paragraphs: Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, commanding general of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, told reporters at the Association of the United States Army's annual meeting that an Army air defense unit has been "earmarked" to support the Golden Dome for America (GDA) missile shield, according to Defense News. He declined to identify the unit but called it "a well-trained organization that we know can meet the demands of Golden Dome for America when the systems are fielded."

Rafferty said current air defense systems are grouped in packages that combine a sensor, an interceptor and a command-and-control system. He described GDA as a way to separate those pieces and link command-and-control systems so that, in his words, commanders can use "any sensor, best shooter, right C2." He said Army air defenders would need some training before the system arrives.

Joint Task Force Gold, a 100-person unit set up in January under U.S. Northern Command and led by Army officers, is also preparing. Deputy commander Col. Kevin Stonerook said the task force has held planning "sprints" since February with about 300 members of the stakeholder community in Colorado Springs to draft a concept of operations and identify open questions. The next sprint is set for the end of October. "There's a lot we still have to figure out," Stonerook said.

Pentagon officials have said they want to field an early version of GDA by the end of next year, with a fuller system built out by 2035. Defense News reported that lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have expressed frustration with slow progress and inconsistent communication from the White House.

The Pentagon requested $17.5 billion for fiscal 2027 through a $350 billion reconciliation package, plus about $400 million in research and development funds in the base budget. Air and Space Forces Magazine reported in September that a dispute over the reconciliation bill could put most of that funding in jeopardy. Rafferty said the Army is "all in" on the project.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance were set to announce a $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, known as WHIP, at an Oval Office event on Tuesday afternoon with the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, according to a White House official quoted by Fox News Digital. The program would pay eligible tipsters up to $30,000 if their information leads to a successful fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action.

The official said the Justice Department will run the program and that tips can be submitted through fraud.gov. A tip alone would not earn a reward; it must lead to a conviction or a significant enforcement action. The Washington Examiner, citing a White House official speaking to NewsNation, described the aim as encouraging whistleblowers to report fraud to the government quickly and easily.

Trump also planned to give independent journalist Nick Shirley a $10,000 check for his work exposing suspected fraud in Minnesota, the official said. Shirley drew national attention in December 2025 with a video questioning whether several Somali-run Minnesota daycare centers were legitimate businesses. The White House credited his reporting with helping prompt a surge of FBI and Department of Homeland Security resources into the state.

Fox News noted that the former CEO of one facility shown in the video, Future Leaders Early Learning Center, pleaded guilty in July to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States. Prosecutors said she stole more than $4.6 million through false child care assistance claims and $850,000 through a federal child nutrition program. Fox also reported that Shirley's work has faced efforts to discredit it; the supplied text did not detail those critics' arguments.

Trump created the task force in March, with Vance as chairman. The executive order directs it to coordinate across agencies to uncover fraud, strengthen eligibility checks and prevent improper payments.

The Justice Department has sent grand jury subpoenas to the office of Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner, a Democrat, in recent days, Fox News reported, citing two sources briefed on the matter. The sources said the subpoenas relate to potential obstruction of justice in the handling of cases before federal judges. Krasner's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the Justice Department declined to comment.

According to the sources, the subpoenas followed a referral from U.S. District Judge Paul Diamond, who more than a month ago sent Krasner and his deputy, Matthew Stiegler, to the Justice Department for possible criminal investigation. Diamond said evidence uncovered in a murder conviction case could constitute false statements, perjury, obstruction of justice and conspiracy. Neither man has been charged.

The dispute centers on Dennis Johnson, who was convicted in 2009 of killing Kenyatta Smith. Fox, citing The Associated Press, reported that the district attorney's office said in a 2022 filing that Johnson was entitled to habeas corpus relief because of ineffective assistance of counsel. Prosecutors later raised potential conflicts involving Stiegler and urged that the matter go to the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office. According to the judge's opinion, Krasner opposed that move and repeatedly said someone from his office needed to stay involved to "protect the office."

Diamond disqualified Krasner and Stiegler from the case but declined to disqualify the whole office. He alleged that they sought to pressure prosecutors into presenting a false narrative to the court and that Krasner warned of "consequences" if staff alerted the court to an internal conflict.
Krasner said at the time that he "respectfully and vigorously" disagreed with the court's findings and conclusions and planned to appeal as soon as the law allows.

Italy's government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and has promised a "firm response from the state" after cost-of-living protests turned into clashes with police, vandalism and looting, The Guardian reported. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the media the response would be "very tough" and that the soldiers would work with prosecutors, according to the Washington Examiner.

Police in Milan detained 271 young people over Saturday and Sunday after hooded youths set bins ablaze, ransacked shops and smashed windows, including near the cathedral. Police said 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, and 28 more were reported to judicial authorities. The violence came from groups on the fringes of an initially peaceful protest. Further demonstrations are planned for Saturday, called by a new social media movement named 17 October.

Italian media reported that Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government plans to approve tougher security measures quickly, including longer preventive detention for minors, a crackdown on youth gangs and bans on gatherings by people deemed a threat to public order. Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool while doing little on education, housing and living conditions, The Guardian said.

In France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said some military forces would be deployed during protests planned for Saturday, mostly to free police and gendarmes for order-keeping duties. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said police numbers would be "massive" and that he wanted an "immediate return to order" after last weekend's riots, in which nearly 2,400 people were arrested. Partial curfews were announced in several cities, including Paris, Bordeaux, Lille and Nice.

Victoria Police have charged Brendan Nugent, 43, of Tarrawingee, over an alleged attack on Australian independent MP Helen Haines. He faces charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police said he will appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday.

Police allege Nugent struck Haines with a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon, and said they will allege the attack was targeted. Haines, 65, who has represented Indi since 2019, was airlifted to the Alfred hospital in Melbourne for emergency surgery. The Guardian reported she has lost one leg and that surgeons were working on Tuesday to save the other. Both outlets said she remains in a critical but stable condition.

Police said a highway patrol officer reached the scene eight seconds after emergency services were called, and that a search warrant was executed at Nugent's Great Alpine Road property. They said the incident appears to be isolated, with no other known threats connected to it. They will keep an enhanced presence in Wangaratta, including the Public Order Response Team.

The BBC reported that local media named the suspect as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father, Rod Nugent, and the father's partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement that they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years." They called it a "shocking and horrific crime," said they would help police "in any way we can," and described Haines as "deeply respected, valued and much loved."
A local barber, Ricky Jefferies, told the BBC he pulled the suspect out of his car. Locals held a vigil at Holy Trinity Cathedral on Tuesday.

Jio Platforms, the telecoms business of Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries, is launching what could be India's biggest initial public offering, The Guardian reported. The company hopes to raise up to 302 billion rupees (about £2.4bn) and is targeting a valuation of 10.3 trillion rupees when shares go on offer from Wednesday, despite a downturn in Indian stocks.

Reliance said in a stock exchange filing last week that the price range is 1,065 to 1,119 rupees a share, with up to 270 million new shares offered. On Monday Jio secured 212 anchor investors, including BlackRock, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Fidelity, Schroders, JP Morgan Asset Management, Franklin Templeton, Invesco and Prudential. Retail investors can buy from Wednesday, and the offer closes on Friday. Reliance is encouraging its more than 400,000 employees to buy, offering a discount of 54 rupees a share.

At the top of the range, Jio would be India's fourth-largest company, behind Reliance, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. That is more than double the 4.9 trillion rupee valuation set in 2020 when Meta and Google invested. It is, however, well below the more than £110bn expected when Jio filed a draft prospectus in the summer. India's Nifty 50 index is down more than 12% this year.

Jio launched in September 2016, led now by Akash Ambani, Mukesh's eldest son. According to Reliance, it gained 16 million subscribers in its first month and passed 100 million within 170 days. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable by triggering a price war. The company plans to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.

Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has predicted a record rise in European air fares next year as airlines face higher fuel bills linked to the Middle East conflict, The Guardian reported. Speaking at a news conference in Brussels, he said fares could rise "by 10, 15, maybe 20%," calling it "the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months."

O'Leary said many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He said Ryanair and many others had hedged their 2026 needs; Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel when the Iran conflict began in late February. But most European airlines, Ryanair included, lack significant hedging from April 2027. "We're 85% unhedged next year," he said. Ryanair's 2027 contract covers 15% of fuel costs at $85 a barrel, while spot prices are about double that.

The Guardian reported that jet fuel prices have soared as the war on Iran has choked off supplies. The airlines body IATA previously predicted prices would be 70% higher across 2026, averaging $152 a barrel against $90 in 2025. EasyJet reported a £105m annual rise in fuel costs in July and said it had hedged 62% of its first-half 2027 needs and 37% of the second half. In October it announced it was cutting 700,000 seats from its winter schedule to save fuel.

In Brussels, O'Leary also said Ryanair is cutting 20 routes and more than one million seats from Belgium this winter after the federal government decided to raise its aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January. Passenger surveys show travellers expect higher fares, but airlines do not know how long consumers can afford them.

A handful of Republican lawmakers have publicly criticized President Donald Trump's approach to Russia and Ukraine, and some have threatened to withhold support for his agenda, according to the Guardian.

The criticism follows two moves. Last week Trump waived sanctions imposed under a law named after the late senator Lindsey Graham, which he signed last month and which was meant to increase financial pressure on Russia. He also announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel fuel. The Guardian says diesel has become more expensive for Americans largely because of Trump's war with Iran.

Over the weekend Trump claimed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "doesn't care" about the impact of Ukraine's strikes on Russia and "doesn't want to end this war and probably never did," because Ukraine receives financial support from Europe. On Monday he suggested it was "time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine." Zelenskyy told Bloomberg he believed Trump was taking steps to "convince Ukraine to capitulate" to Russian demands, and he reaffirmed Ukraine's partnership with the US on social media.

Nebraska congressman Don Bacon, who is leaving office, called the actions "absolutely disgraceful" and told CNN the president's leverage in Congress is "shot." He said he was unwilling to back priorities such as a victory arch or a White House ballroom. Pennsylvania congressman Brian Fitzpatrick said lawmakers would "demand accountability" and could take "punitive budgetary action." Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina said she would put pressure on Russia instead. Senator Bill Cassidy and former senator Mitt Romney also criticized the direction of policy.

Some lawmakers had already raised concerns after Ukrainian officials said Starlink access was restricted last week. Musk hinted that the US government controlled that access. Zelenskyy also accused Washington of withholding intelligence about a Russian missile attack on Sunday, the third such accusation. The page text does not include a White House response to these criticisms.

Voters in Alberta have decisively chosen to remain in Canada. According to unofficial Elections Alberta results reported by the Guardian, with nearly 1.9 million votes counted, roughly 76 percent backed staying and 24 percent backed starting a process toward separation. The BBC reported that preliminary results showed more than two-thirds choosing Canada.

The ballot question asked whether Alberta should remain a province or whether its government should begin the legal process required to hold a binding referendum on separating. It was one of 10 questions on Monday's ballot. Five of the others dealt with immigration and four with the constitution, and early results suggest most will pass, including proposals for more provincial control over immigration. Elections Alberta said the remaining counts could take days.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called it a "great result" and said Albertans "chose unity." Premier Danielle Smith, who opposed separation but went ahead with the vote, said Albertans voted for "a stronger Alberta in a united Canada." She had said that if voters chose to remain, no binding separation referendum would be held while she was in power.

Separatist leaders said they would carry on. Jeffrey Rath called the vote a "first step" and told the BBC his movement was "continuing to move forward." He told Global News he would push for a special meeting of the United Conservative Party to remove Smith, whom he called an "avowed federalist." Another separatist leader, Keith Wilson, said at least a quarter of Albertans feel the province needs to be treated better.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said there is "still work to be done" on how Western Canada is treated by Ottawa. Pollster David Coletto told the Guardian that most Albertans have grievances with the federal government but few want to end the relationship. Smith said she would address Albertans on Tuesday about the way forward.

Sudan's army has been accused of carrying out several drone strikes that reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens traveling to a funeral, the BBC reported. The casualty figures come from sources and officials rather than independent confirmation.

The Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), said sources put the death toll at 150 from Sunday evening strikes in two places in West Kordofan state. It said a truck carrying around 200 mourners was hit as it arrived in Al-Dabab, killing 145 people, and a funeral tent was also hit, killing five. It said 150 people were injured. Army drones also bombed a market in Al-Mujlad, where the numbers of dead and injured were not yet known. The group said the drones were likely launched from the army-held city of Kadugli.

On Monday, drones hit Amiet Market near Abyei, a disputed area between Sudan and South Sudan. The region's information minister said 153 people were killed. A military source told the BBC the army carried out that attack and described the market as a fuel supply site for the RSF. The army has not responded to the allegation about the other strikes, but has said it does not attack civilians. BBC Verify said satellite images show extensive burnt buildings at the market.

South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest, and there are fears the conflict could spill across the border. UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said the UN was alarmed by the drone strikes, noting that 20 million people face acute hunger. Separately, AFP reported a drone strike near Khartoum's airport killed four people, including three children.

Kenya has confirmed a ninth Ebola case, according to a Ministry of Health statement on Tuesday. The patient is a 24-year-old man who was already in quarantine when he fell ill. The ministry said he was isolated at the first sign of illness, tested, and started on treatment as soon as his positive result was confirmed.

He was a close family member of Kenya's first Ebola patient. That patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda to Kenya and died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5. Health Director-General Patrick Amoth said all nine cases belong to one cluster and that there is no evidence of transmission outside it. He said eight patients are stable and responding well to treatment, and that 134 of 135 contacts have been traced and quarantined.

Amoth said most contacts in quarantine had stayed well through the 21-day monitoring period and could return home from October 25. The ministry appealed to communities to welcome them back, saying they pose no risk of infection. It also said no infections had occurred inside quarantine facilities. Despite the cases, Kenya has not imposed restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, and authorities say the country remains open for business.

The cases come amid the outbreak in the DRC, where there have been more than 9,000 cases and 4,000 deaths since May. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control calls it the second-largest epidemic on record. Al Jazeera notes it has been hard to contain because there is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of the virus.

The French government has summoned online platforms to emergency meetings as it tries to contain rioting and looting and to stop stolen goods being resold, according to Wired. Digital affairs minister Anne Le Hananff met social media firms on Tuesday to remind them they must moderate content, including livestream video, so that it does not show violence or encourage people to break the curfew, BFM reported.

A day earlier, a separate meeting with reselling platforms ended with what small business minister Serge Papin called a signed agreement. Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta and TikTok attended. Papin said the platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen during the protests, and send the government reports on their actions, the first within 48 hours. eBay said it removes fake ads and can permanently suspend seller accounts. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta and TikTok did not respond to Wired's request for comment.

Wired said a review of TikTok found that searching "blocus," meaning blockade, showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, and that the term was being used to promote a second round of protests on October 24. TikTok attached an "evolving situation" notice to the search.

The unrest began as peaceful demonstrations over living costs and strained public services, Wired reported. Rioting and looting of more than 1,500 shops followed over the weekend. Interior minister Laurent Nunez admitted police "lost control" in some cities, and authorities say more than 2,400 people have been arrested.

The Washington Examiner reported that Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told parliament that "far-left" and "ultra-left" groups had forged an "insurrectionary plan" against the government, after being briefed by intelligence services. It said Monday night was calmer and the government is preparing for further unrest. The text available does not include any response from the groups named.

French President Emmanuel Macron has secured commitments for an extra 200,000 tonnes of diesel a month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, according to the French presidency. The Elysee announced the deals on Tuesday as Macron arrived in Qatar on a three-day Gulf tour that also includes Kuwait. Together with deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France now has commitments for 295,000 tonnes a month, just over 10 percent of its consumption.

The presidency said Kuwait has also made commitments to supply diesel and kerosene to Mayotte and Reunion, with shipments routed via Oman to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has blockaded the strait during the eight-month conflict with the US and Israel, and diesel has been among the hardest-hit fuels. France has released 10 million barrels of diesel from its reserves, aiming to cut prices by 12 to 18 cents a litre from next month. TotalEnergies chief Patrick Pouyanne, who is traveling with Macron, said, "We are not going to run out of diesel in February."

The trip follows a weekend of violent protests in France. Fox News reported that Macron left for Kuwait on Sunday after denouncing the "unbridled" violence, and that he defended the trip by saying fuel prices were one cause of the unrest. Fox said he faced criticism from both sides. Marine Le Pen said France was "caught in a vice between violence and impotence." Jean-Luc Melenchon accused the government of relying on "inaction and police brutality."

Analyst Andreas Krieg told Al Jazeera the deals fit a wider pattern of Gulf states seeking closer ties with European countries as the US increasingly sidelines both. Fox said officials have arrested more than 2,500 people and that Macron declined his interior minister's resignation. France's presidential election is approaching.

The United Kingdom will use RAF Typhoon fighters to help protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks, the Guardian reported. The jets will fly defensive missions over Saudi cities and critical infrastructure and will attempt to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones. The Guardian described it as the most significant military mission approved so far by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The Ministry of Defence said the aircraft "will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis." It did not state how many jets will be sent. The UK will also provide military advisers and an Atlas A400M transport aircraft. An existing commitment to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi fighter jets with an RAF Voyager has been extended by 90 days.

The Iran-aligned Houthis began an offensive in Yemen in September that has escalated into a wider regional conflict, with attacks on Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's officially recognized government. Thirteen people were killed this month when a missile hit King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, the deadliest incident since September. The war has killed 19 people in Saudi Arabia so far, according to the Guardian.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the Houthi attacks "absolutely despicable" and said the UK was "responding to protect civilians." The announcement came days after he met US counterpart Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon to discuss the Houthi escalation among other issues.

The Guardian noted some concern that the UK risks being seen as closely aligned with the unpopular US war on Iran. It said the intervention was partly justified on the grounds that instability in the Middle East is driving up energy prices and the cost of living. RAF Typhoons also flew defensive missions against Iranian and proxy missiles and drones in the spring and summer.

Turkiye has submitted to its parliament for ratification a three-way defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The agreement was signed on August 7 and contains 16 articles, according to the document seen by Reuters and cited by Al Jazeera.

Article 1 commits the signatories to use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity. Article 2 says that if one party suffers armed attack or military aggression, the others "shall immediately provide assistance." Al Jazeera noted this resembles Article 5 of the NATO treaty. Each country, however, will decide the scope and nature of its support after an objective assessment of what is needed, within its available resources.

Other articles cover defense industry cooperation, intelligence sharing, logistics, joint training, and the fight against terrorism. The pact would create a defense committee of foreign and defense ministers from the three states. Other countries could join only with the approval of all three founders. The agreement runs for 10 years, after which any country can withdraw.

Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate "deterrence measures" under the pact and to deploy forces rapidly to Saudi Arabia to counter Houthi attacks. The Houthis have recently struck Saudi oil facilities and Riyadh's main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition has launched air attacks on Houthi positions. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday that Turkiye is "surrounded by a ring of fire."

Al Jazeera's Resul Serdar said ratification could take "quite some time" and may bring heated debate, even though the ruling coalition needs only a simple majority. He said ratification alone would not send Turkish troops, which would need further legislative steps. A source told Reuters that parliament's foreign affairs commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday.

More than half a million male mosquitoes carrying a parasite called wolbachia have been released in Barcelona, New Scientist reports. It describes this as the first large-scale release of its kind in Europe. When the males mate with females, the eggs will not hatch. The aim is to reduce the number of mosquitoes in the city and the risk of infections such as dengue.

The project involves the pest-control company Rentokil and a Google project called Debug. Rubén Bueno Mari of Rentokil said the main concern in Europe is the Asian tiger mosquito, which can spread dengue and chikungunya and is established in 16 European countries, including Spain. Because it can breed in tiny amounts of water, such as rainwater in discarded rubbish, he said conventional methods like putting insecticide in large pools work poorly.

Releases began in mid-August after regulators approved them. Each week, 80,000 males are produced at Debug's facility in Miami and flown to Spain. Rentokil and Debug are funding the releases, which will stop in mid-November and resume in May. Wolbachia is passed down in eggs and can stop infected males from fertilising uninfected females' eggs, which makes the males effectively sterile. In small earlier trials in Rome, according to Rentokil and Debug, releases cut the number of viable eggs by nearly 90 per cent.

One difficulty is separating males from females accurately, since releasing fertile females could spread wolbachia locally and undermine the method. Debug uses an automated process based on AI image recognition. Bueno Mari could not say what share of females get released and said the trials are meant to help find out. He said the insects are the same strain already present in Spain, so no new strains can be introduced.

In Singapore, a study published earlier this year concluded the technique cut dengue cases by 70 per cent. Debug is seeking permission for releases in Florida and California. Bueno Mari said there is no single magic solution and called the approach a promising addition to integrated mosquito management.

Uzbekistan became the 77th signatory of the Artemis Accords at a ceremony in Samarkand on Monday, according to NASA. The country committed to the practical principles that guide safe, transparent and responsible civil space exploration. Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov signed for Uzbekistan during a visit by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said Uzbekistan joins at a pivotal moment. He said President Trump has directed NASA to build a Moon Base and establish an enduring presence on the lunar surface, and called Uzbekistan a welcome addition to a growing coalition.

NASA said Uzbekistan has been building a national space program aimed at advancing its space industry and its role in global space forums. Uzbek students are working to develop and launch the country's first CubeSat, a small satellite technology demonstration, by 2028. In early October, NASA officials met representatives of Uzbekistan's Ministry of Digital Technologies and its space agency, Uzcosmos, at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Türkiye, where they discussed civil space cooperation. Uzbekistan is scheduled to host that annual event in 2028.

NASA and the State Department created the Accords in 2020 with seven other founding nations, responding to growing interest in lunar activity by governments and private companies. According to NASA, signers commit to explore peaceably and transparently, to render aid to those in need, to enable access to scientific data, to avoid interfering with others' activities, and to preserve historically significant sites and artifacts. NASA said it expects more countries to sign in the months and years ahead.

The United States has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop buying services and products from Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and to remove them from government IT systems, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.

DHS cited national security concerns tied to the company's operations in China. The order raised concerns about DeepSeek's handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law.

China pushed back. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes "overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues," according to an official briefing. "We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises," the spokesperson added.

The order builds on earlier steps. A law passed in December 2025 targeted DeepSeek's use in intelligence's national security systems, and the latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.

DeepSeek has faced scrutiny since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares. A September report said the US accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems. OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about alleged distillation by DeepSeek.

Separately, Bloomberg reported last week that China is considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models. DeepSeek's own response to the US order was not reported in the source text.
HSBC chief executive Georges Elhedery said investors should be selective about AI data centers, even as he called the technology transformational. He spoke to CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday.

Elhedery described AI as "a major enabler to re-engineer and reimagine all our businesses, all our activities," and said it would give staff greater productivity and help "re-engineer the bank." On infrastructure, though, he urged discernment. "One has to be selective," he said. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."

S&P Global ranked HSBC the seventh-largest bank in the world and the biggest lender in Europe last year, with assets close to $3 trillion. The London-based bank is both a financier and operator of data centers, and its 2025 annual report said its customer base spans data centers and the AI sector.

McKinsey says global data center spending could reach $7 trillion by 2030, with Big Tech increasingly using private credit and debt to fund the buildout. CNBC reported that AI borrowing is becoming a source of tension in financial markets as the cost of capital rises. JPMorgan Chase estimated earlier this year that $4.1 trillion in AI-related debt will be issued by the end of the decade.

Mohamed El-Erian of Allianz, speaking at the GZERO Summit in London this month, said hyperscalers raised $200 billion in bond financing last year and may raise a trillion this year. He called them "yield insensitive" and "spread insensitive" and pointed to competition for financing between governments and AI-related companies.

Meta has paused the sharing feature in Muse, its AI agent, after researchers reported Monday that shared conversations could expose sensitive information. Meta told Ars Technica it is reviewing the report and considering changes to how the links can be discovered.

Security firm Claroc said it enumerated 6,800 share links. After opening a few hundred, it found material apparently not meant to be public, including a loan application with the amount requested, a company's internal revenue review, and a staff vacation calendar listing dozens of employees. "It took one query," the researchers wrote.

Claroc said all the links use one domain and put the conversation title in the subdomain, so public DNS records make them searchable. The firm said many AI assistants share by public link, but Muse's are easy to find because the title sits in the web address.

Claroc co-founder Asaf Aprozper said he reported the findings through Meta's bug bounty program on October 8 and got no reply. Meta said it opened the program so researchers could raise scenarios and help it improve the product.

Separately, TechCrunch, citing Sensor Tower, reported that Muse reached 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of them in the US, and hit 2.5 million daily active users on October 16. The app is available only in the US and Canada.

Ars also reported that researcher Patrick Wardle found a vulnerability three weeks after launch that let other apps on the same device take control of a Muse account. Meta downplayed it because exploitation required an already compromised device.

TikTok employees repeatedly warned executives about risks the platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR and reported by TechCrunch and The Verge. Staff were frustrated by how leaders responded, including to concerns about sexual exploitation and suicide-related content.

The depositions, filed in federal court in March, are part of multi-district litigation begun in 2022 that combines hundreds of lawsuits against TikTok, Meta, Snap and Google. The suits allege the companies knew their platforms harm children and failed to disclose the risks.

Reagen Maher, who held senior safety and investigations roles between 2021 and 2024, described flagging "transactional sexual content" to then-CEO V Pappas, involving minors stripping on TikTok Live in exchange for "gifts" that can be converted into real currency. In an internal chat he wrote that "senior leaders know about this issue." Former head of safety Eric Han described harmful algorithm "rabbit holes" in 2020 with a "real contagion effect" regarding suicidal ideation.

NPR also reported that minors exploited loopholes to access age-restricted content and hide their activity from parents. The documents show TikTok did not survey users' ages out of concern it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.

A TikTok spokesperson said the citations were "cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers" and mislead the public. The spokesperson said the company has invested billions of dollars in Trust & Safety and offers more than 50 preset teen safety settings, including Family Pairing.
TikTok has settled several of the cases before trial.
Google Cloud said services are recovering after a power event at its London cloud region, europe-west2, disrupted UK banks, businesses and courts on Tuesday.

Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC confirmed disruption to some services. The banks did not directly link the problems to Google, but Revolut said its issue came from a third party and that customers' money and data were safe. Customers also reported problems with Royal Mail and DPD, and HM Courts and Tribunals Service said an issue affected the video platform used for remote hearings. The Guardian reported glitches on the NHS app.

According to the Guardian, Downdetector reports peaked around 9am and were somewhat resolved by mid-afternoon. Google said the issues had been mitigated for most customers and that it would publish an analysis once its internal investigation is complete. A Google spokesperson said the disruption occurred at a third-party facility.
Customers described the effects. Revolut user Rachael Ellen said she could not pay for parking. Guy Baybutt of The Veg Box Company said the firm could not process orders or book parcels with DPD.

The outage came exactly a year after an Amazon Web Services outage that the Guardian said lasted about 15 hours and was far larger. Prof Feng Li of Bayes Business School said it was not yet clear what caused the power problem, adding that "failures will happen" and what matters is how far they spread. Internet infrastructure expert Michał Woźniak said it was unreasonable for a handful of companies to hold so much sway. The Guardian said up to 60% of UK government infrastructure is hosted on cloud services.
Two robotics startups have announced funding at valuations above $1 billion, according to TechCrunch.

Reliable Robotics, based in Mountain View, California, raised $115 million: $90 million in equity led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The money extends its Series D to $275 million and pushes its valuation beyond $1 billion. It has raised $380 million to date. The company develops autonomous flight technology for existing aircraft and is seeking FAA certification.

CEO Robert Rose expects certification of its first system in 18 to 24 months. That system handles engine startup, taxiing, takeoff and landing while the pilot stays aboard. Moving the pilot to a ground station is at least three years away, and Rose expects its solid-state collision-avoidance radar to be certified by the end of 2027.

Eka Robotics closed a $150 million Series A at a $1.45 billion post-money valuation, led by a16z and F-Prime. It was founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja. Its system pairs a force-sensitive gripper with a vision-force-action model trained through physics simulation and reinforcement learning.

Eka says its robot picks up about 1,500 objects of up to 1 kg per hour, compared with about 600 for a human, and succeeds more than 95% of the time. Those figures are the company's claims. Kris Hauser of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said the robot adapted to many objects without retraining. a16z's Raghu Raguram predicted superhuman performance in many dexterous tasks over the next few months.
Gecko Robotics announced Tuesday that the US Navy is raising the ceiling of its AI maintenance contract to up to $300 million, just six months after the initial agreement.

The sources differ on the starting point. Defense News describes an initial five-year, $54 million indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity deal covering 18 Pacific Fleet ships. The Robot Report cites an initial $71 million contract with the Navy and the General Services Administration and says the ceiling was quadrupled.

The Pittsburgh-based company uses drones, wall-climbing robots and fixed sensors to gather data on hulls, decks, welds and components. AI tools then flag current and potential structural problems that may be invisible to the eye. Gecko claims its technology can save up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and find issues up to 50 times faster, cutting inspections from months to days. Those are company claims. CEO Jake Loosararian said the conversation is "no longer about experimental technology."

A key part of the expansion is Komodo, which scans deck coatings without digging into them and produces a heatmap of corrosion and material thickness. That lets the Navy plan repairs before a ship enters dry dock, something previously possible only after maintenance began.

The Navy has set a goal of 80% fleet readiness by 2027. The Government Accountability Office reported in December 2024 that readiness of amphibious warships fell to 46% between 2011 and 2020, and Defense News said the rate reportedly dipped to 41% in August 2025. Adm. Daryl Caudle wrote that reaching the goal requires shorter maintenance cycles, more spare parts, better training and targeted upgrades.
An Air Force F-22 Raptor controlled a YFQ-44A Fury, an Anduril-made Collaborative Combat Aircraft, in flight earlier this month, the Air Force announced.

The F-22 pilot served as an airborne "quarterback," giving high-level directives. The unmanned, semi-autonomous aircraft's onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed them in real time, performing in-flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks, according to the Air Force release.

Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the achievement shows what is possible when the service is aligned with industry on delivering capability to the warfighter at unprecedented speed. Personnel from the 412th Test Wing, 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron, 309th Software Engineering Group and other units collaborated on the demonstration. The service plans to use the data to inform software integration, developmental testing and further CCA concepts.

The test follows other milestones. The Air Force has said it intends to field 500 combat-ready, semi-autonomous systems by 2032, with an overall fleet of 1,000. In July, the Fury carried out its first live-fire test, an end-to-end, beyond-line-of-sight strike against a simulated target at Edwards Air Force Base, California.

General Atomics' FQ-42A Vengeance was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nevada, last month for continued test and evaluation. Anduril has yet to announce which base will house the Fury, but Creech airmen have already used the company's aircraft in an Agile Combat Employment exercise, flying sorties and building tactics and procedures for integrating CCAs into the force.

China built more than twice the naval tonnage of the United States in 2024-25, according to the World Defense Shipbuilding report published by Euronaval, with data compiled by Flottes de Combat and the French maritime industry association Gican. Chinese yards produced 636,208 tons of combat ships in the two years through December 2025, against 270,509 tons for the US.

China accounted for more than a third of global naval tonnage built. Worldwide, 1.47 million tons of combat vessels were built, up from 959,671 tons in the prior two years, and the value of construction rose to $123.9 billion from $81.8 billion. Chinese construction was valued at $43.5 billion and US construction at $26.8 billion.
The picture has reversed from 2022-23, when Chinese yards built 202,520 tons and US yards 245,703 tons.
The US fleet of combat vessels over 200 tons still outweighs China's: 3.11 million tons as of Jan. 1, 2026, against 1.44 million. Two years earlier the figures were 3.22 million and 1.3 million.

Gican general director Philippe Missoffe said at a Paris press briefing that the report shows a substantial expansion of naval forces and shipbuilding, including more nuclear-powered attack submarines. US lawmakers and congressional researchers have warned that China's shipbuilding capacity, combined with US delays and bottlenecks, could hurt America's ability to keep pace.

Russia ranked third with 149,056 tons, followed by India with 76,430 and Italy with 53,700. Turkey, France, Japan, South Korea and Romania completed the top 10. The Euronaval show opens in Paris on Nov. 3, with more than 40% more exhibitors than in 2024.
